analysis.one_liner: Exemts shipping between Puerto Rico and U.S. ports from the Jones Act's U.S.-built, U.S.-crewed vessel rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: four Republican senators backed it and it sat on the Senate calendar until the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The Jones Act requires that ships carrying goods between U.S. ports be built in the United States, mostly owned by U.S. citizens, and mostly crewed by Americans. That makes the short route to Puerto Rico the domain of a handful of U.S.-built ships, and shipping there costs far more than shipping to nearby foreign islands. This bill would carve Puerto Rico out of those rules permanently, letting any qualifying vessel carry cargo to the island. It was introduced in the Senate in the weeks after Hurricane Maria and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor time.
analysis.who_benefits: Puerto Rico's three million residents and its retailers, who pay elevated shipping costs on nearly everything they buy; the bill would let more ships and lower-priced carriers serve the island, and this is likely to reduce the cost of consumer goods.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the coastwise laws so that Puerto Rico is listed as an exception, meaning vessels carrying merchandise between Puerto Rico and other U.S. ports would no longer have to be U.S.-built, mostly U.S.-owned, and mostly U.S.-crewed.
Passenger vessels between Puerto Rico and U.S. ports were already exempt from these requirements; the bill extends that same treatment to cargo ships.
With more vessels eligible to serve the island, competition on the route could increase and shipping costs, which feed into the shelf price of food and goods, could fall.

analysis.who_pays: U.S.-flag shipping companies that hold the Puerto Rico route, the U.S. shipyards that build their vessels, and American merchant mariners whose jobs depend on the protected route.

drawbacks.text: The exemption could shift cargo from U.S.-built vessels to foreign carriers, reducing demand for American shipyards and for U.S. mariner jobs on the route. This is the core good-faith objection the protected industry raises to any Jones Act repeal.

Supporters of the Jones Act argue the U.S.-built, U.S.-crewed fleet serves as a domestic shipping capacity the military can draw on in wartime; a permanent exemption shrinks the pool of vessels and crews available for that purpose.

The existing U.S.-flag carriers on the Puerto Rico route have invested in vessels built to meet these rules; opening the route to foreign competition could undercut that investment and lead them to reduce service or exit the market.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Puerto Rico residents, the upside is concrete and everyday: cheaper shipping means cheaper groceries and goods on an island where freight costs are a major driver of prices. The costs fall on a much smaller group — shipyards, U.S.-flag carriers, and mariners — and the military-readiness argument is real but indirect. On balance the bill offered a targeted, meaningful cost-of-living relief at the expense of a well-defended protected market.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and placed directly on the Senate calendar, but no committee took it up, no senator ever brought it to the floor, and the Congress ended with it still sitting on the calendar.

narrative.text: Senator John McCain introduced the bill in the Senate on September 28, 2017, with three Republican cosponsors — Mike Lee, James Lankford, and Jeff Flake.
The introduction came less than two weeks after Hurricane Maria devastated Puerto Rico in September 2017 and put the island's high shipping costs in the national spotlight.

Rather than going to committee, the bill was read the second time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 232, on October 2, 2017 — a placement that allows floor action but does not require it.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, and the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 with the bill still on the calendar.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The U.S.-flag shipping companies and shipyards that keep the protected Puerto Rico route are better off, since their exclusive market is intact. Puerto Rico's temporary 10-day Jones Act waiver during the hurricane crisis expired, and the island's permanently higher shipping costs stayed in place.

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.role: U.S. Senator from Arizona; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 28, 2017, during the post-Hurricane Maria recovery, to permanently exempt Puerto Rico from the Jones Act.

for.name: Sens. Mike Lee, James Lankford, and Jeff Flake
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it three cosponsors.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote; it sat on the legislative calendar until the Congress ended.

against.name: U.S.-flag shipping companies and shipbuilders
against.role: Jones Act carriers and maritime industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed exemptions and repeal of the Jones Act, defending the protected domestic shipping market through industry groups and lobbying.

against.name: President Trump
against.what_they_did: Said he supported the Jones Act rather than changing it, and his administration authorized only a temporary 10-day waiver for hurricane relief supplies instead of backing a permanent exemption.

sides.party_line_note: No chamber ever voted on the bill, so the parties' positions were never recorded; all four sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, while support for protecting the Jones Act has historically crossed party lines.

industries.industry: U.S.-flag shipping carriers on the Puerto Rico route
industries.note: These carriers hold a protected route where only a handful of U.S.-built ships can legally serve Puerto Rico, and the exemption would have opened the route to competition. The route's high costs are paid by island consumers in the price of goods.
Jones Act rules guarantee demand for expensive U.S.-built vessels on domestic routes including Puerto Rico; the exemption would shrink that guaranteed market.

industries.industry: U.S. merchant mariners and maritime labor
industries.note: The rules require U.S. crews, protecting mariner jobs on domestic routes; opening the Puerto Rico route to foreign-crewed vessels would put some of those jobs at risk.

industries.industry: Puerto Rico retailers, shippers, and consumers
industries.note: Lower shipping costs on the route would flow directly into lower prices for food and goods on the island, which is the bill's central purpose.
